passage: On Friday, Aditi saw the senior by the staircase glaring at her. He stood in the middle of the landing, arms folded, and as she came closer he stepped sideways to block the way, sneering, "Where do you think you're going?" Her stomach tightened and her mouth went dry. She didn't answer back. She turned around, walked to the crowded corridor where her friend Ishita was, and said quietly, "Come with me to the staff room. Someone is blocking the stairs and I feel unsafe." Ishita didn't hesitate. They went together, and Aditi told the teacher on duty exactly what had happened, without exaggerating.

qa.q: Where did the senior block Aditi's way?
qa.a: He blocked her way on the landing by the staircase.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when the senior sneered at her?
qa.a: She felt unsafe and frightened, shown by the tight stomach and dry mouth, and she chose not to answer back.

qa.q: Why was going to a teacher with Ishita a wise choice?
qa.a: Hostility is a warning to disengage, stay near others and involve a trusted adult, not to retaliate.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when Aditi asked Ishita to come along?
qa.a: Ishita may have felt worried for Aditi but also trusted, since Ishita went at once and gave support.

grounding: A teen notices a peer glaring and blocking the way, feels unsafe, and disengages, stays near others and tells a trusted adult.

"You look weird. What happened?" Rukmini said, putting down her book as Kamal dropped his bag in the hall.
"There's a boy at the cycle stand. He stares at me every day like he wants a fight. Today he stood in front of my cycle and wouldn't move."
"Did you say anything?"
"No. My hands were shaking. I wanted to shove him, honestly."
"Good that you didn't. Next time, stay near other people and don't wait around alone. And tell your class teacher today, not next week."
"Won't that make it worse?"
"Maybe he'll be embarrassed. Maybe not. But you shouldn't handle this by yourself." She squeezed his shoulder. "I'll come to school with you tomorrow if you like."

qa.q: Where does the boy stare at Kamal every day?
qa.a: He stares at Kamal at the cycle stand.

qa.q: What does Kamal's wish to shove the boy suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests fear mixed with anger, since his hands were shaking, but he held back.

qa.q: What would you advise Kamal to do first?
qa.a: Tell his class teacher today and stay near other people, as Rukmini says, instead of retaliating or handling it alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini to hear this?
qa.a: She is probably worried and protective, which is why she offers to go to school with him. 🙂

grounding: A teen faces a peer glaring and blocking his way and is advised to disengage, stay near others and involve a trusted adult.

passage:
In Class 9, a senior named Vikram started doing something every day. When I walked to the library, he'd step into the corridor and stand in my way. Arms folded. Staring. Once he muttered, "Watch yourself." His friends smirked.
He never touched me. But my stomach knotted every time I turned that corner.
My first thought was to say something back, or shove past. My brother said I should. But Vikram was bigger, and his friends were always there.
So I did what felt safer. I stopped walking alone. Ankita came with me every time. We took the longer route past the staff room.
And on Friday I told Mrs Ghosh, our class teacher. She listened, wrote down the days and what he'd said, and said, "Thank you. This isn't something you should handle alone." She spoke to his class teacher that same afternoon.
It stopped the next week.
- Tanuja

qa.q: What did Vikram mutter once?
qa.a: "Watch yourself."

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling each time Tanuja turned that corner?
qa.a: Tanuja felt frightened and unsafe, stomach knotting at the sight of Vikram blocking the way.

qa.q: Which of Tanuja's choices were protective?
qa.a: Not retaliating, walking with Ankita on a route near the staff room, and telling Mrs Ghosh, who recorded it and acted that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt walking with Tanuja every day?
qa.a: Ankita was probably concerned and loyal, glad to help Tanuja feel safer.

grounding: The account shows a teenager reading glaring and blocking as hostility, disengaging, staying near others and involving a trusted adult.

passage:
PE teacher's note - Varun, Tuesday
Bidisha from Class 10 came to me after the last period. She said that for four days, three boys from another section had been waiting near the cycle shed. When she went to unlock her cycle, they glared, sneered and stood in front of it so she couldn't get out. Yesterday one of them kicked her tyre.
She said, "I wanted to push them. But there were three." I told her she was right not to fight back.
I thanked her for coming straight to me. We agreed she would leave with her friends from now on and park near the gate, where the guard is. I walked her to the shed today.
I have informed the vice-principal and the boys' class teacher, and their parents will be called in this week. I told Bidisha to come to me at once if anything else happens.

qa.q: How many days had the boys been waiting near the cycle shed?
qa.a: For four days.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling about the boys at the cycle shed?
qa.a: Bidisha felt unsafe and threatened, and angry enough to want to push them, but frightened because there were three of them.

qa.q: What steps kept Bidisha safer?
qa.a: Not retaliating, leaving with friends, parking near the guard, and telling Varun, who walked her to the shed and reported it to other staff and parents.

qa.q: How might the boys' parents feel when they are called in?
qa.a: They may feel surprised or embarrassed, and would need to take the hostility seriously.

grounding: The PE teacher's note shows a teenager reading glaring and blocking as hostility and involving a trusted adult instead of retaliating.

passage:
Wednesday
There's a boy on the school bus, I don't know his name, who's started glaring at me every morning. Today he put his bag on the only empty seat and sneered, "Not for you." When I stood near him, he pushed his shoulder into mine, hard, like he wanted me to push back.
I wanted to. My fists were tight. But I remembered Dadi saying, "When someone's looking for a fight, don't give them one."
So I walked to the front and stood near the driver instead. Madhuri shifted and made space for me next to her. She whispered, "He did that to Sonu last week too."
At home I told Mummy everything. She didn't say "ignore it." She called the school bus in-charge that same evening, and they're moving him to the other route and checking the bus camera.
I feel better. Still a bit shaky.
- Kamal

qa.q: What did the boy put on the empty seat?
qa.a: He put his bag on the only empty seat.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when the boy pushed a shoulder into Kamal?
qa.a: Kamal felt angry and unsafe, fists tight, sensing the boy wanted a fight.

qa.q: Which choices protected Kamal?
qa.a: Not pushing back, moving near the driver and Madhuri, and telling Mummy, who called the bus in-charge that same evening.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have seen the boy's behaviour?
qa.a: Madhuri seemed to see it as a pattern of hostility, since he had done the same to Sonu, and made space to keep Kamal near her.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager reading glaring, sneering and shoving as hostility, disengaging, staying near others and involving a trusted adult.
